A similar idea was brought up awhile back by someone else already, /u/MarkW (who has apparently deleted his account and left). He wanted a system where each subverse was a republic of sorts, with users voting on who the moderators are. I argued with him extensively about it.

Let me ask you this:

What incentive will there be for anyone to put their effort into their sub if they cannot retain control over it?

Imagine being the person who creates the sub, spending a ton of time curating it and growing it, then one day, being stripped of your power and control and having it taken away from you. With that possibility in mind, no one is going to devote too much effort into it. No one is going to have the will to implement unpopular measures (that may be ultimately beneficial despite being unpopular) because then they might get a petition against them.

Because it's all too easy for someone to criticize someone elses idea for its flaws, let me give you an alternative idea that does not require human intervention.

Get rid of the current "default" system where there is only one /v/politics (using /v/politics as an example).

Let there be several (or even numerous) /v/politics and let users choose between them. In other words, now the /v/politics compete with each other for users. They will ranked according to user activity and users would be able to readily see what they are in a public listing.

Each /v/politics can function like its own mini-dictatorship, although it doesn't have to (a group of people can create their own subverse where they can vote on their moderators if they want to.)

Because people want their subs to be popular, even if it is a dictatorship, they aren't going to implement any bad policies or do anything to ruin that. If they do, there will be a migration away from it.

It's essentially a "market solution" where people vote with their feet and chose to patronize the sub that they think is best. This may change from time to time, as the subs are ranked. Subs may fall out of favor and/or new subs can rise to power.

You would expect to see a wide variety of subs for a given topic. Some may choose to implement the republic/petition type of system (and it might work for them), but it may not work elsewhere if it is inefficient compared to another system. Voat, the site itself need not decide and pick any one. It will just allow for all possible configurations to exist, and whatever works will come forth.

I wouldn't want a republic in the subverses, just a way for wronged Voaters to be righted. What if somebody actually was banned for subscribing to a subverse that the moderator didn't approve of - there needs to be a way to deal with cases like that.

[IAMA request] Someone who suffers from migraine / cluster-headache / similar illnesses
I have migraines. Was there something specific you wanted to know?

1. How often do you get migraines?

  2. What, in your opinion, is the exact difference between migraines and a serious headache, apart from migraines being more chronical?

  3. Do you ever feel sick to the stomach because of it?

  4. Have you ever recognized a structure of when it happens, like in certain situations or on certain days or does it just occur randomly?

  5. Does the weather have an effect on it?

This is why I started this IAMA request in case you'd like to read

Thanks for your answer!

Edit: 6. Do usual meds agains headache work against migraines for you?

1) I get between 1 to 3 during a normal week.

2) The differences? I feel more of a pressure in my head with a migraine - any change in movement sets of the pounding/throbbing worse. I've described the feeling as if my skull was a rotting melon. I also suffer more noise and light sensitivity with migraines.

3) I often get a low grade nausea with migraines, but only become physically ill every couple of months. If you can ever avoid throwing up will your head is trying to explode, do it. I end up in tears afterwards. And usually end up at the ED because I can't even keep my meds down for relief.

4) Causes are multiple. Hormonal is a big one. Certain chemicals/scents - I can't go to a nail salon at all because I end up with a migraine within minutes due to nail polish remover. A regular headache can develop into a migraine if I don't treat it, but that's not always a guarantee. And oddly enough, with a let up of stress. I knew that I could count on migraines after a school term ended and I knew I would get one after I took my state boards, oh and wasn't that one a doozy!!

5) Weather is a definite factor for me. Barometric changes/weather shifts/extreme heat all make me more likely to have a migraine.
Seems like I forgot to say "thank you" before, as posts like these are very informative and helpful. So.. Thanks for your answer.
6) Regular meds do little for my migraines. At best they may knock the pain down a notch. I take a triptan for the migraine itself and toradol for pain relief.
Thank you for all your interesting answers!

That may be a decent argument for not requiring labeling. But it is a terrible argument to prevent labeling.

I don't mind GMO foods, but I have no problem with them being labeled so people know what they're buying. How is having to have a GMO label different from having to list all the chemicals in (for example) Coke Zero?

How is having to have a GMO label different from having to list all the chemicals

The reason is that GMOs are not "meaningfully" different than nonGMO. The problem is that GMO labeling costs money and makes a statement. Companies would have increased cost from tracking and testing their food to prove if it's GMO free. The label would also state that there is a difference between GMO and nonGMO, that's forcing a company to say something which violates their free speech. The difference with ingredients lists is that it is "meaningful" if my doctor wants me to avoid sugars or I have a rare allergy to a particular additive knowing if a product contains sugar or that additive is "meaningful".

There was a similar thing that happened with cell phones. San Francisco (of course) passed a law that required cellphone dealers to publicly list how much radiation the phone puts off. This was to let customers choose low radiation phones, however because the amounts were negligible this labeling would force cellphone makers to lower their radiation levels to compete without actually making them healthier. Now it's not illegal to list the radiation exposure from a phone, it's just illegal to force companies to say it.
